claim: Cystic fibrosis is one of the most common recessively inherited disorders caused by the deficient CFTR gene that encodes a chloride channel.
source: Cystic fibrosis (CF), which primarily targets the respiratory system, is one of the most common recessively inherited disorder caused by the deficient CFTR gene that encodes a chloride channel (Stoltz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stoltz et al., 2015, which provides external scholarly support for this statement.

claim: The main features of CF airway diseases include mucus obstruction and repetitive infections and inflammation.
source: The main features of CF airway diseases include mucus obstruction and repetitive infections and inflammation, which often lead to severe airway remodeling and respiratory failure (Regamey et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Regamey et al., 2011.

claim: CF symptoms emerge as early as the fetal stage.
source: It has been reported that CF symptoms emerge as early as the fetal stage, indicating that alterations of airway development can have a profound impact on the respiratory function later in life (Gosden and Gosden, 1984; Larson and Cohen, 2005; Regamey et al., 2011; Verhaeghe et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Gosden and Gosden, 1984; Larson and Cohen, 2005; Regamey et al., 2011; Verhaeghe et al., 2007).

claim: Mouse mutants that lack Cftr do not exhibit airway defects similar to those found in cystic fibrosis patients.
source: Mouse mutants that lack Cftr do not exhibit airway defects similar to those found in cystic fibrosis patients (Lavelle et al., 2016; McCarron et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lavelle et al., 2016 and McCarron et al., 2018.

claim: Other chloride channels, such as calcium-activated chloride channel (CaCC), may compensate for the lack of Cftr in mice.
source: This led to the hypothesis that chloride channels may play species-specific roles and that other chloride channels, such as calcium-activated chloride channel (CaCC), may compensate for the lack of Cftr in mice (Clarke et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis and is supported by a citation to Clarke et al., 1994.

claim: Ano1, also known as Tmem16a, is a CaCC in the Anoctamin/TMEM16 family.
source: Ano1, also known as Tmem16a, is a CaCC in the Anoctamin/TMEM16 family.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about Ano1/Tmem16a that is part of established scientific knowledge.

claim: Ano1 regulates intracellular chloride homeostasis.
source: Ano1 regulates intracellular chloride homeostasis (He et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to He et al., 2017.

claim: Ano1 is required for survival.
source: Ano1 regulates intracellular chloride homeostasis (He et al., 2017) and is required for survival (Lek et al., 2016; Rock et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lek et al., 2016 and Rock et al., 2008.

claim: Mouse mutants that lack Ano1 exhibit abnormal trachea morphology.
source: mouse mutants that lack Ano1 exhibit abnormal trachea morphology (Rock et al., 2008; Rock et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rock et al., 2008 and Rock et al., 2009.

claim: ANO1 is a candidate drug target in the modulation and management of CF.
source: Given its function as a chloride channel in the airway, ANO1 is a candidate drug target in the modulation and management of CF (Amaral and Beekman, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Amaral and Beekman, 2020.

claim: A massive expansion of the secretory cell population was observed in Ano1-/- knockout airway at postnatal day 0 (P0).
source: Using fluorescently labeled Jacalin, a plant-based lectin that recognizes airway glycoproteins and mucin components (Ostedgaard et al., 2017), as well as antibody against SCGB1A1, a low-molecular-weight protein enriched in airway secretory cells, we observed a massive expansion of the secretory cell population in Ano1-/- knockout airway at postnatal day 0 (P0) (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, using fluorescently labeled Jacalin and SCGB1A1 antibody staining.

claim: Jacalin-positive mucus substance was observed in Ano1-/- knockout airway lumen.
source: In addition, Jacalin-positive mucus substance was observed in Ano1-/- knockout airway lumen (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At P3 and P5, PAS and Alcian Blue staining demonstrated strong mucus obstruction of the respiratory tract and alveolar simplification in Ano1-/- neonatal lung.
source: At P3 and P5, Periodic Acid–Schiff stain (PAS) and Alcian Blue staining of airway histological sections consistently demonstrated strong mucus obstruction of the respiratory tract and alveolar simplification in Ano1-/- neonatal lung (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C,D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C,D,E using PAS and Alcian Blue staining.

claim: Wild-type trachea at P2 showed directional flow at 0.90 ± 0.22 μm/s from the distal to the proximal trachea.
source: At P2, wild-type trachea showed directional flow at 0.90 ± 0.22 μm/s from the distal to the proximal trachea (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—video 1.

claim: Ano1 mutants showed minimal and sometimes reversed flow at 0.42 ± 0.18 μm/s.
source: In contrast, Ano1 mutants showed minimal and sometimes reversed flow at 0.42 ± 0.18 μm/s (Figure 1C,D; Figure 1—video 2), significantly slower than the velocity observed in littermate controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—video 2.

claim: There was a significant increase in the number of secretory cells in the mutant airway compared to wild-type.
source: Immunostaining of SCGB1A1 showed a significant increase in the number of secretory cells in the mutant airway compared to wild-type (Figure 1E,F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A using SCGB1A1 immunostaining.

claim: The numbers for ciliated cells were unaffected in Ano1-/- mutant airway compared to littermate wild-type.
source: Based on the expression of Centrin2-GFP, the numbers for ciliated cells were unaffected in Ano1-/- mutant airway compared to littermate wild-type (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A using Centrin2-GFP expression.

claim: TEM analysis revealed subcellular defects in mutant neonatal epithelial cells, including short microvilli, dilated ER lumen and accumulation of large amorphous vesicles.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis revealed subcellular defects in mutant neonatal epithelial cells, including short microvilli, dilated ER lumen and accumulation of large amorphous vesicles (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The wild-type single-cell embryonic and neonatal atlas largely agrees with previously published atlases of the adult airway in the expression of marker genes for major epithelial cell types.
source: Our wild-type single-cell embryonic and neonatal atlas largely agrees with previously published atlases of the adult airway in the expression of marker genes for major epithelial cell types (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Montoro et al., 2018; Plasschaert et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published data (Montoro et al., 2018; Plasschaert et al., 2018) and shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Major cell types of the developing airway and molecular markers associated with each cell type are highly conserved between mice and humans.
source: Taken together, we observed that major cell types of the developing airway and molecular markers associated with each cell type are highly conserved between mice and humans (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Coordinated differentiation programs of luminal cell types, including ciliated and secretory cells, were initiated between E15 and E16 in wild-type mice.
source: In wild-type mice, coordinated differentiation programs of luminal cell types, including ciliated and secretory cells, were initiated between E15 and E16 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Spdef and Creb3l1, two transcription factors that promote the secretory cell fate, and Foxj1, a transcription factor essential for the motile ciliated cell formation, were upregulated at E16 compared to E15.
source: Spdef and Creb3l1, two transcription factors that promote the secretory cell fate (Chen et al., 2009; Gregorieff et al., 2009) and Foxj1, a transcription factor essential for the motile ciliated cell formation (You et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2008), were upregulated at E16 compared to E15 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and citations to Chen et al., 2009; Gregorieff et al., 2009; You et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2008.

claim: The number of cycling cells was diminished as differentiated cells began to emerge.
source: Conversely, the number of cycling cells, reflected by a calculated cell cycle score, was diminished as differentiated cells began to emerge (Figure 3C; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: At E15, the broad presence of Trp63 but low level of Krt5, and the marked expression of Id2, Id3, Wnt7b, and Cldn6 indicate that undifferentiated cells dominate the Epcam+ epithelium.
source: At E15, the broad presence of Trp63 but low level of Krt5, and the marked expression of Id2, Id3, Wnt7b, and Cldn6 indicate that undifferentiated cells dominate the Epcam+ epithelium (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from gene expression patterns shown in Figure 3D.

claim: When luminal cells begin to emerge at E16, Trp63+ basal cells switch to a different expression program, consisting of Krt5, Krt15, Aqp3, and Aqp4.
source: When luminal cells begin to emerge at E16, Trp63+ basal cells switch to a different expression program, consisting of Krt5, Krt15, Aqp3, and Aqp4, which may play important roles in the epithelial barrier function (Kreda et al., 2001; Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and a citation to Kreda et al., 2001.

claim: The immature secretory program showed a pronounced expression of Cited1, a transcription cofactor that activates TGF-β and BMP signals.
source: At E16, in addition to Spdef and Creb3l1, the immature secretory program showed a pronounced expression of Cited1, a transcription cofactor that activates TGF-β and BMP signals (Plisov et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by data and a citation to Plisov et al., 2005.

claim: The neonatal secretory program was distinguished by elevated expression of Gp2 and Tff2, which are important mucosal proteins and markers for goblets cells found in the adult airway.
source: Conversely, the neonatal secretory program was distinguished by elevated expression of Gp2 and Tff2, which are important mucosal proteins and markers for goblets cells found in the adult airway (Hase et al., 2009; Montoro et al., 2018; Nikolaidis et al., 2006; Wills-Karp et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by data and citations to Hase et al., 2009; Montoro et al., 2018; Nikolaidis et al., 2006; Wills-Karp et al., 2012.

claim: The neonatal secretory program includes expression of Sftpd, which encodes a surfactant protein and is involved in the innate immune program.
source: as well as Sftpd, which encodes a surfactant protein and is involved in the innate immune program (Brandt et al., 2008; Mackay et al., 2016; Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and citations to Brandt et al., 2008 and Mackay et al., 2016.

claim: The immature secretory program includes gene modules required for protein folding and trafficking, which are critical for the secretory pathway.
source: The immature secretory program includes gene modules required for protein folding and trafficking, which are critical for the secretory pathway (Trombetta and Parodi, 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis (Figure 3E) and a citation to Trombetta and Parodi, 2003.

claim: The mature secretory program features processes involved in the regulation of cell division.
source: while the mature secretory program features processes involved in the regulation of cell division (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Both embryonic and postnatal ciliated cells expressed Foxj1.
source: In our dataset, both embryonic and postnatal ciliated cells expressed Foxj1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Immature ciliated cells were characterized by Foxn4, Ccna1, Ccno, Mcidas, as well as by Shisa8.
source: Immature ciliated cells, which are predominantly present during embryogenesis, were characterized by Foxn4, Ccna1, Ccno, Mcidas, as well as by uncharacterized markers, such as Shisa8, which is an auxiliary subunit for the AMPA receptor and a member of the CKAMP glutamate receptor family required for synaptic transmission (Farrow et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data and a citation to Farrow et al., 2015.

claim: The immature ciliated program includes pathways involved in protein synthesis.
source: The immature ciliated program includes pathways involved in protein synthesis (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: RNA FISH analysis of Mcidas and Shisa8 showed colocalizations with Foxn4 and Foxj1 in E16 wild-type trachea.
source: RNA FISH (fluorescent in-situ hybridization) analysis of Mcidas and Shisa8 showed colocalizations with Foxn4 and Foxj1 in E16 wild-type trachea (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Postnatal mature ciliated cells upregulate Sntn, which encodes a phosphatidylserine binding protein localizing to the tip of motile cilia.
source: In contrast, postnatal mature ciliated cells upregulate Sntn, which encodes a phosphatidylserine binding protein localizing to the tip of motile cilia (Kubo et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by data and a citation to Kubo et al., 2008.

claim: Postnatal mature ciliated cells express various membrane receptors, such as Cdhr3 and Ldlrad1, which are involved in rhinovirus infection.
source: and express various membrane receptors, such as Cdhr3 and Ldlrad1, which are involved in rhinovirus infection (Basnet et al., 2019; Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and a citation to Basnet et al., 2019.

claim: The mature ciliated program highlights molecular pathways that are involved in axoneme assembly, apical junction organization, as well as cilia movement and motility.
source: Overall, the mature ciliated program highlights molecular pathways that are involved in axoneme assembly, apical junction organization, as well as cilia movement and motility (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A population of epithelial cells expressing both the ciliated-cell module and the secretory-cell module was identified in the postnatal mouse dataset.
source: In the postnatal mouse dataset, we identified a population of epithelial cells expressing two gene modules, the ciliated-cell module and the secretory-cell one (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The presence of a cilia-secretory hybrid cell type was validated by FISH analysis of Foxj1, Gp2 and Prr18 in neonatal tracheal samples.
source: Using neonatal tracheal samples, we validated the presence of a cilia-secretory hybrid cell type by FISH analysis of Foxj1, Gp2 and Prr18, a novel ciliated cell marker (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Based on immunofluorescence staining, hybrid cells expressed FOXJ1 and a secretory cell marker SCGB1A1.
source: Based on immunofluorescence staining, these hybrid cells expressed FOXJ1 and a secretory cell marker SCGB1A1 (Figure 4C; Rawlins et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C and citations to Rawlins et al., 2009 and Zhang et al., 1997.

claim: TEM revealed that a subset of luminal cells exhibit both characteristic cilia axoneme and intracellular vesicles.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) revealed that a subset of luminal cells exhibit both characteristic cilia axoneme and intracellular vesicles, indicating that hybrid cells indeed possess two sets of machineries required for motility and secretion, respectively (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Pofut1-/- mutants lacked secretory cells that are only expressing Gp2, but exhibited double positive Foxj1- and Gp2-expressing hybrid cells.
source: Pofut1-/- mutants lacked secretory cells that are only expressing Gp2, but exhibited double positive Foxj1- and Gp2-expressing hybrid cells, indicating that hybrid cells are derived from a ciliated cell linage (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: About 50% of Foxj1Cre labeled mGFP+ cells at P0 to P1 expressed cytoplasmic SCGB1A1.
source: About 50% of Foxj1Cre labeled mGFP+ cells at this stage expressed cytoplasmic SCGB1A1 at P0 to P1, suggesting that a major proportion of the neonatal hybrid cells are likely derived from a ciliated cell lineage (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Many of the airway disease associated genes are expressed by cells of the airway epithelium.
source: Many of the airway disease associated genes are expressed by cells of the airway epithelium, including modifier loci for CF severity, such as Muc20 and Ehf, as well as risk genes shared between COPD and pulmonary fibrosis, such as Fam13a and Dsp.
evidence: This claim is supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Scores for mucosal hyperplasia are higher in cilia-secretory hybrid cluster, and are also elevated in T cells, endothelial cells, and vascular smooth muscles.
source: Scores for mucosal hyperplasia are higher in cilia-secretory hybrid cluster, and are also elevated in T cells, endothelial cells, and vascular smooth muscles (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by scGPS analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The PCD scores are higher overall for ciliated cells and cilia-secretory hybrid cells.
source: The PCD scores are higher overall for ciliated cells and cilia-secretory hybrid cells, confirming that ciliated cells are primary targets for PCD.
evidence: This claim is supported by scGPS analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The cilia-secretory hybrid cells show prominent enrichment scores in multiple airway conditions.
source: Interestingly, the cilia-secretory hybrid cells show prominent enrichment scores in multiple airway conditions (Figure 4E), indicating a critical role of this hybrid cell state in airway function and pathogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by scGPS analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mutant epithelial cells significantly downregulated Retnla, Itln1, and Chil4.
source: Significant downregulation of these markers was observed in all Ano1-/- mutant luminal cells (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutant epithelial cells expressed high levels of Cxcl17 and Ccl20.
source: Conversely, mutant epithelial cells expressed high levels of Cxcl17 and Ccl20 (Figure 5C), two potent chemotactic factors for lung macrophages (Burkhardt et al., 2014; Schutyser et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and citations to Burkhardt et al., 2014 and Schutyser et al., 2003.

claim: Mutant epithelial cells significantly downregulated NF-κB inhibitors Nfkbia and Nkfbiz.
source: Mutant epithelial cells significantly downregulated NF-κB inhibitors Nfkbia and Nkfbiz (Figure 5B,C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the NF-κB signaling may be abnormally regulated in the absence of Ano1.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ano1-/- mutant immune cells upregulated a set of immune modulators, including Saa3.
source: Consistent with the abnormal expression patterns of barrier defense genes, Ano1-/- mutant immune cells upregulated a set of immune modulators, including Saa3, that are expressed during inflammation (Eklund et al., 2012; Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and a citation to Eklund et al., 2012.

claim: Ano1-/- mutants displayed an expansion of the secretory cell population across all time points analyzed, from E16 to P1 and P4.
source: Ano1-/- mutants displayed an expansion of the secretory cell population across all time points we analyzed, from E16 to P1 and P4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ano1 mRNA can be detected as early as E12 in the respiratory epithelium.
source: Ano1 mRNA can be detected as early as E12 in the respiratory epithelium (Rock et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rock et al., 2008.

claim: Using RNA FISH analysis and scRNAseq, Ano1 expression was confirmed in undifferentiated mouse airway epithelium as well as in differentiated secretory cells.
source: Using RNA FISH analysis and scRNAseq, we confirmed Ano1 expression in undifferentiated mouse airway epithelium as well as in differentiated secretory cells (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA FISH and scRNAseq data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: CFTR mRNA was broadly distributed in the mouse airway at E15 as well as in human fetal airway epithelium at GW15.
source: Similarly, CFTR mRNA was broadly distributed in the mouse airway at E15 as well as in human fetal airway epithelium at GW15 (Figure 6A,B,C)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A,B,C.

claim: CFTR was expressed in secretory cells associated with the surface epithelium and submucosal glands at GW21-23.
source: and expressed in secretory cells associated with the surface epithelium and submucosal glands at GW21-23 (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The percentage of cells from the Krt4+ immature secretory state markedly increased in Ano1-/- mutants compared to wild-type mice.
source: Compared to wild-type mice, the percentage of cells from the Krt4+ immature secretory state markedly increased in Ano1-/- mutants (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The expansion of Krt4+ immature secretory cells in neonatal mutant trachea was confirmed via KRT13 immunofluorescent staining.
source: We confirmed the expansion of these Krt4+ immature secretory cells in neonatal mutant trachea via KRT13 immunofluorescent staining, given that Krt13 is paired with Krt4 in airway epithelial cells (He et al., 2015; Montoro et al., 2018; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and citations to He et al., 2015 and Montoro et al., 2018.

claim: In Ano1-/- mutants, the percentage of Sostdc1+ basal cells was reduced.
source: In Ano1-/- mutants, the percentage of Sostdc1+ basal cells was reduced (Figure 7C)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Sostdc1 expression was significantly downregulated in Ano1-/- mutants.
source: and Sostdc1 expression was significantly downregulated (Figure 7D,E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D,E,F.

claim: Cell cycle scores were comparable between wild-type and Ano1-/- mutants for basal and secretory cell states identified at E16.
source: Changes associated with cell states were unlikely caused by altered cell proliferation, because cell cycle scores were comparable between wild-type and Ano1-/- mutants for basal and secretory cell states identified at E16 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Embryonic removal of Ano1 from the airway endoderm resulted in mucus cell hyperplasia and an expansion of Krt13+ immature secretory cells.
source: we used Shhcre, which is expressed in all Shh-expressing endodermal cells during embryogenesis (Swarr and Morrisey, 2015), and found that embryonic removal of Ano1 from the airway endoderm resulted in mucus cell hyperplasia and an expansion of Krt13+ immature secretory cells (Figure 7G; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, and a citation to Swarr and Morrisey, 2015.

claim: Removal of Ano1 from basal progenitor cells resulted in a differentiation bias toward the secretory lineage during the regeneration phase.
source: In a polidocanol induced airway injury model (Liu et al., 2006), removal of Ano1 from 3 week-old mice similarly resulted in a differentiation bias toward the secretory lineage during the regeneration phase (Figure 7H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7H and a citation to Liu et al., 2006.

claim: The percentage, transcriptome profiles, and developmental trajectory of ciliated cells are comparable between wild-type control and Ano1 mutants.
source: Overall, the percentage, transcriptome profiles, and developmental trajectory of ciliated cells are comparable between wild-type control and Ano1 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B,C,D.

claim: Ano1-mediated chloride homeostasis maintains a Sostdc1-expressing progenitor pool within the epithelial basal cells.
source: Based on the aforementioned changes in the cellular composition and molecular profiles between wild-type and Ano1 mutant tracheal epithelial cells, we propose that Ano1-mediated chloride homeostasis maintains a Sostdc1-expressing progenitor pool within the epithelial basal cells, loss of which results in secretory hyperplasia at least partially due to an accumulation of intermediate secretory cells with elevated levels of Krt4 and Krt13 (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented in the study.

claim: Lineage specification of ciliated cells appears unaffected in the absence of Ano1.
source: Lineage specification of ciliated cells, on the other hand, appears unaffected in the absence of Ano1.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that ciliated cell development is comparable between wild-type and mutants.

claim: All cell types identified in the mouse trachea have corresponding orthologous cell types in humans.
source: Importantly, all cell types identified in the mouse trachea have corresponding orthologous cell types in humans, indicating that the two species employ conserved gene regulatory programs to build the large airway during embryogenesis.
evidence: This claim is based on comparative analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Most monogenic disease genes implicated in PCD are specifically expressed in ciliated cells.
source: Our assessment of enrichment patterns for selected airway disease genes using scGPS confirmed that most monogenic disease genes implicated in PCD are specifically expressed in ciliated cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by scGPS analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Susceptibility loci for COPD are expressed in both epithelial and stromal cell types.
source: In contrast, susceptibility loci for COPD are expressed in both epithelial and stromal cell types, consistent with the pleiotropic presentations of complex-trait airway disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Foxn4 is required to promote motile cilia formation in Xenopus epidermis.
source: Foxn4 is required to promote motile cilia formation in Xenopus epidermis (Campbell et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Campbell et al., 2016.

claim: Foxn4 expression is very transient during frog embryogenesis.
source: and its expression is very transient during frog embryogenesis (Briggs et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Briggs et al., 2018.

claim: Foxn4 expression peaks transiently at E16 in the mouse trachea as ciliated cells begin to emerge.
source: Our data indicate that Foxn4 expression peaks transiently at E16 in the mouse trachea as ciliated cells begin to emerge, supporting a central role of Foxn4 in promoting motile ciliogenesis in mammals.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: During embryogenesis, epithelial cells upregulate multiciliated gene modules and secretory gene modules to initiate a massive differentiation process between E15 and E16.
source: During embryogenesis, epithelial cells upregulate multiciliated gene modules and secretory gene modules to initiate a massive differentiation process between E15 and E16.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: After the animals are born and start breathing, tracheal epithelial cells upregulate a set of mucosal cytokines, antibacterial effectors, and Th2 immune response genes that are critical for the maturation of barrier function.
source: After the animals are born and start breathing, tracheal epithelial cells upregulate a set of mucosal cytokines, antibacterial effectors, and Th2 immune response genes that are critical for the maturation of barrier function.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The neonatal hybrid cell state is likely derived from a ciliated cell lineage.
source: Our data indicate that this neonatal cell state is likely derived from a ciliated cell lineage.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The hybrid state appears to be very rare during the adult homeostatic state and cannot be induced by chemically-triggered airway regeneration.
source: The hybrid state appears to be very rare during the adult homeostatic state and cannot be induced by chemically-triggered airway regeneration (Rawlins et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rawlins et al., 2007.

claim: A cluster of cilia-secretory hybrid cells are found in the human inflammatory airway.
source: In contrast, a cluster of cilia-secretory hybrid cells are found in the human inflammatory airway, indicating that neonatal airway may share similar immune status to the inflamed adult airway (Ordovas-Montanes et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2011; Tyner et al., 2006; Vieira Braga et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ordovas-Montanes et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2011; Tyner et al., 2006; Vieira Braga et al., 2019.

claim: Trans-differentiation of ciliated cells into goblet cells can be induced by IL-13.
source: Supporting this notion, trans-differentiation of ciliated cells into goblet cells can be induced by IL-13, a major cytokine involved in allergy and inflammatory response (Turner et al., 2011; Tyner et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Turner et al., 2011 and Tyner et al., 2006.

claim: Ano1 in the undifferentiated epithelial cells plays an essential role in maintaining airway progenitors by limiting the differentiation of basal cells into the secretory lineage.
source: First, Ano1 in the undifferentiated epithelial cells plays an essential role in maintaining airway progenitors by limiting the differentiation of basal cells into the secretory lineage.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the study.

claim: Persistent expression of Ano1 in differentiated airway epithelial cells controls the normal status of the neonatal mucosal immunity.
source: Second, persistent expression of Ano1 in differentiated airway epithelial cells controls the normal status of the neonatal mucosal immunity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the study.

claim: A shift in the expression of antimicrobial genes and proinflammatory modules in Ano1 mutants indicates that these mutants may be more prone to infection and inflammation.
source: A shift in the expression of antimicrobial genes and proinflammatory modules in Ano1 mutants indicates that these mutants may be more prone to infection and inflammation, which result in secondary pulmonary dysplasia (Davidson and Berkelhamer, 2017; Shahzad et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from gene expression data and supported by citations to Davidson and Berkelhamer, 2017 and Shahzad et al., 2016.

claim: Intracellular chloride, regulated by chloride channels, has been implicated in vesicle trafficking and plays a role in regulating plasma membrane dynamics.
source: Intracellular chloride, regulated by chloride channels, has been implicated in vesicle trafficking and plays a role in regulating plasma membrane dynamics (Bradbury et al., 1992; He et al., 2017; Stauber and Jentsch, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bradbury et al., 1992; He et al., 2017; Stauber and Jentsch, 2013.

claim: Inactivation of CFTR in humans and Ano1 in mice, respectively, lead to congenital abnormalities of the airway.
source: Inactivation of CFTR in humans and Ano1 in mice, respectively, lead to congenital abnormalities of the airway, raising the possibility that perhaps intracellular chloride homeostasis, modulated by these two chloride channels, represents a conserved component for mammalian airway development.
evidence: This claim is based on the data presented in the study and represents a conclusion.

claim: Ano1 and CFTR are expressed in orthologous cell types of mouse and human airway epithelium, respectively.
source: Because Ano1 and CFTR are expressed in orthologous cell types of mouse and human airway epithelium, respectively, our work provides a tractable animal model for understanding the roles of chloride channels in human airway development and pathogenesis.
